abstract:
Prefix reuse improves LLM inference by sharing the KV cache of common prompt prefixes. This helps only if the scheduler can execute a matched branch in the current worker round. Schedulers assume that a matched prefix is ready, which holds for full attention but fails for hybrid LLMs. There, a branch (the consumer) may need recurrent state that another branch (the producer) is still computing in the same round. The native scheduler stops its waiting-queue scan at this blocked consumer, and the resulting head-of-line blocking creates execution bubbles: idle batch slots that independent work could fill. We introduce RadixFlow, which decouples prefix matching from state readiness. Its state-ready traversal turns a global scan barrier into a local wait: only the consumer is blocked until the next round, while feasible independent branches keep filling the batch under the native state check. On five hybrid models, RadixFlow lowers mean latency by 3% to 24% and worker rounds by 11% to 44% at almost unchanged reuse. On the larger Qwen3.5 models, ablations show that most of the gain comes from traversal, which adds little on a full-attention control. Heavier rounds limit how much of this saving reaches latency.

All techniques have been implemented and integrated into vllm-jev.

sections.body: Hybrid LLMs need recurrent and convolutional state at a prefix match, so a consumer branch can wait for a producer in the same worker round. The native vLLM scan stops at the blocked consumer, leaving idle rows that independent branches could fill. RadixFlow's state-ready traversal blocks only the consumer, which is rechecked in the next round, and keeps selecting feasible branches. On five hybrid models, mean latency falls by 3% to 24% and worker rounds by 11% to 44%, with prefix reuse within 0.03 percentage points of Radix. Traversal drives most of the gain on the larger Qwen3.5 models. The remaining rounds carry more work, so their cost limits how much of the round reduction reaches latency.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Hybrid LLMs make a cache-matched branch wait for a same-round producer, and the native scan stalls behind it.

sections.body: PagedAttention shares KV pages, RadixAttention indexes exact prefixes, and hybrid caches keep the recurrent components needed at a reuse boundary. Scheduling systems balance reuse, load, and waiting through request ordering or batch formation. RadixFlow keeps that storage policy and uses the native state check to pick executable work. It acts inside a round: a same-round dependency changes which branches are selected, without changing their native order or bypassing a state read. The section also cites bounded dynamic batching for the timer controls and tree-aware batching for measuring per-round cost. Appendix K gives the broader comparison.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prefix-caching systems decide what state can be reused, while RadixFlow changes only which executable branches a round selects.

sections.body: A branch can run only if its prefix matches, its state is usable at the resume boundary, and it fits the round's row and token budgets. A readiness outcome is Ready, Blocked when a same-round producer is still writing the needed state, or Other for budget overflow and unrecognized failures. An avoidable execution bubble exists when a round has unused rows and some arrived branch is Ready. The objective is the mean flow time over logical requests, measured from arrival to completion of their last branch. For the Figure 1 workload, a four-round layout attains the capacity bound, and the formal proofs appear in the appendices.
sections.heading: Problem Formulation
sections.headline: Batch construction must admit only branches with a matching prefix, usable state at the resume boundary, and fitting resources.

sections.body: State-ready traversal replaces the prefix-stop rule. It scans branches in native order, selects those that are Ready through the native allocator, and moves Blocked consumers to a wait queue that stays registered for the next round. Other outcomes keep their native handling. Flexible admission releases arrived branches earlier, with a 5 ms admission deadline, about 9% of the 52.95 ms native mean worker-call interval on Qwen3.5-0.8B. For fixed state, the batch contains every branch that prefix-stop selects. This guarantee assumes monotone readiness and no Other stop. The extra scan visits each blocked consumer once per pass, so the extra work grows linearly with the number of inspected branches.
sections.heading: RadixFlow
sections.headline: RadixFlow blocks only the consumer of a same-round dependency and keeps scanning for independent work that fits.

sections.body: Table 1 compares Radix with timer controls, Radix+Flex, RadixFlow, and RadixFlow+Frag, each over 9306 requests per model. On the hybrid models, RadixFlow lowers latency and rounds while reuse stays within a fraction of a point of Radix. The full-attention control, Qwen3-8B (FA), shows 16.4 seconds for both Radix and RadixFlow. Table 2 shows denser rounds and earlier first selection on every hybrid model. On Qwen3.5-27B, host cost per thousand scheduled tokens falls from 183 to 175 ms, and total host-wrapper time falls by 3.8%. On Qwen3.5-9B, the cost shift absorbs about 60% of the round credit. Qwen3.5-27B is overloaded at five requests per second, so queueing dominates its latency.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: RadixFlow lowers mean latency and worker rounds on the hybrid models while prefix reuse stays nearly unchanged.

sections.body: In hybrid LLM serving, a prefix match alone does not make a branch runnable. RadixFlow blocks only the consumer of a same-round dependency and continues to select independent work that fits the round. The conclusion recommends that schedulers treat such dependencies separately from memory pressure, since a blocked consumer needs only a recheck in the next round. The reported gains are measured on the frozen configurations described in the experiments section.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: A cache match is not yet a runnable branch, so schedulers should separate same-round dependencies from memory pressure.

sections.body: The evaluation focuses on candidate-conditioned prefill with one generated token, under a frozen model, budget, and arrival setting. The reported measures are worker-call timing and decoded-output agreement. Load sweeps, production scheduling, and finer dependency traces are left to extend this setting. Appendix N records the comparison scope.
sections.heading: Limitations
sections.headline: Results cover candidate-conditioned prefill with one generated token under frozen settings, without load sweeps or production traces.

sections.body: Experiments use public benchmark inputs and publicly available model weights under their terms. Exact-prefix namespaces remain isolated, and no approximate semantic cache reuse is introduced. Failed and incomplete artifacts are kept, and final summaries are produced only after identifier, ownership, and token-accounting checks. AI assistance was used for implementation and manuscript revision. The authors remain responsible for the reported evidence and claims. Appendix F documents the native state contract and shared implementation primitives.
sections.heading: Ethical Considerations
sections.headline: Experiments use public benchmark inputs and public model weights, and the paper discloses assistance used in implementation and revision.

sections.body: Appendix A explains the design choices and the alternatives that were not adopted. Appendix B gives the replay and calibration protocol, including native-only parameter selection and cache isolation. Appendix C defines the token and round accounting and separates three clocks. Appendix D gives the full stream model and the capacity bound, and Appendix E proves the traversal result. Appendix N audits the baseline and replay sensitivity. Decoded agreement with Radix ranges from 98.477% to 99.995% for RadixFlow, and the audit retains the differing strings.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix covers design rationale, replay protocol, timing semantics, stream proofs, and audits of baselines and output agreement.
